newsitem.title: INDIA: India Congress leader sees early end to crisis.
newsitem.headline: India Congress leader sees early end to crisis.

text.p: A leader of India's Congress party said on Sunday he was optimistic agreement could be reached with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's defeated United Front and saw an early end to the country's political crisis.

Both Deve Gowda's 15-party coalition and Congress president Sitaram Kesri, his ally-turned-foe, were battling to keep their deputies together amid reports of mounting dissent, prompted by poll fears and lurking political uncertainty.
Congress party chief Sitaram Kesri has insisted that Deve Gowda step down as United Front leader, a demand the United Front has resolutely opposed.
Congress parliamentary deputy and former minister Rajesh Pilot said he was optimistic that the two groups would sink their differences and hammer out a compromise very soon.

"I am very sure both the groups, having the national interest in mind, are ready to sacrifice individuals...in the political interest. I think we can find a solution even as early as the next two or three days," Pilot told Reuters Television.
Pilot, whose party withdrew its make-or-break support to the United Front after Deve Gowda refused to resign, said afterwards that he was referring to individual interests, not people.

Congress precipitated Deve Gowda's fall when it voted against his government in a confidence motion on Friday. But neither Pilot's party nor the United Front (UF) is keen on elections that would ensue if no party was able to muster a majority in India's hung parliament.

"Today also I believe that both UF and Congress should open up to each other, talk frankly keeping the national interest in mind, keeping the political stability in mind," Pilot said. No member of parliament wanted fresh elections, he added.
"So compulsion from members of parliament and the necessity of the national interest today would bring us together and we will come out with some sort of solution," Pilot said.
The United Front denied reports of dissent among its coalition partners over Deve Gowda's leadership.
"Deve Gowda will be the leader," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy said after Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party held its political affairs committee meeting in New Delhi on Sunday.
"It (Janata Dal) expresses solidarity with the United Front in today's situation," he added. "Deve Gowda will be the leader and of course we'll go along with the United Front."
State radio quoted Deve Gowda as saying the alliance would face elections, which the Congress would like to avoid.
But party members said pressure was mounting on Deve Gowda to help avert elections even if it meant stepping down.
"The MPs do not want elections," Pilot said. "The compulsion from every party of MPs is, 'No elections, please come round and talk.'"
Other disgruntled party leaders said privately they would press for Kesri's sacking at a meeting of the party's Congress Working Committee scheduled for Monday at 8 p.m. (1430 GMT).
The alliance's official position that it would not support either Congress or the right-wing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in forming a government could change, one of them said.

Leaders of four regional parties which are constituents of the United Front met to chalk out a strategy and agreed to support Deve Gowda, setting to rest speculation that they would chart their own course.
